candidates.text:
Selling Oculus to Facebook in 2014 gave me money for helicopter flight lessons and developing a seastead called SLAB with a 1,000 year design life.

The goal was to be cheaper than land and absent state/local laws that cripple critical American industries like metal processing, medical research/treatment, desalination, oil refining, chemical engineering, and more.  Me and a few close friends cashed it up at a $1B valuation back in 2017, and while it still has a long way to go, there has been significant progress towards my goal of reviving manifest destiny and westward expansion.  At a time when most of the seasteading community wanted to escape the US and smoke pot, this was the one project explicitly designed to make America stronger, a relief valve for ill considered or outdated rules and regulations.

I am only talking about it now because a few media outlets got wind of me and some friends topping up the coffers and plan on calling SLAB my new floating AI datacenter project. It is way cooler than that, way older than that, and I hate looking like a hype-chasing consensus loser, so now you have to read this tweet.

candidates.text:
This painting just sold for $85.8 million, a new auction record for Kandinsky.

In 1964, the Guggenheim sold ‘Betonte Ecken’ for £22,000. The museum said it didn't have the wall space.

If you've wondered how a museum lets a painting like this go, and how it comes back as a record, strap in.

#1 ::: A record waiting to fall

Kandinsky's auction record was $44.8 million, set at Sotheby's in 2023.

Tonight at Christie's in New York, the bidding opened at $54 million.

The record was gone on the first bid.

Three bidders chased it. The hammer came down at $74 million.

With fees, $85.8 million. Almost double the old record.

Christie's had guaranteed the painting to the seller, and an outside backer had already placed an irrevocable bid.

So it was always going to sell. The only question was how far past $44.8 million it would go.

#2 ::: The story

Hilla Rebay, a German baroness and painter living in New York, buys this canvas.

It's the first Kandinsky oil she ever owns.

She sends it to her New York home and writes to the painter Rudolf Bauer: "I really like it very much—it is most beautiful in the light."

Rebay was Solomon R. Guggenheim's adviser. On her advice he started buying abstract painting in depth, and she became the first director of the museum that turned into the Guggenheim.

In 1941 the painting entered the Guggenheim Foundation.

Then 1964.

The museum owns 170 Kandinskys. It sends 50 of them to Sotheby's in London, all in one sale.

The official reason: not enough room to show them.

Harry Guggenheim, the museum's president, put it this way: "Before, it was a bit like misers going down into the cellar and counting the gold."

All 50 paintings brought in $1,502,200 together.

This one went for £22,000.

In 1986 it came up again, at Sotheby's New York. $1 million at the hammer.

The buyer kept it for 40 years. Until tonight.

#3 ::: So, why this painting?

Christmas Eve, 1921. Kandinsky and his wife Nina arrive in Berlin. They lost their property in the 1917 revolution. They never go back.

Six months later he's teaching at the Bauhaus.

He paints this in Weimar, between December 1922 and January 1923. It's 130 x 130 cm, and he logged it as number 247 in his own handlist.

It's one of the first canvases where his loose, cosmic swirls give way to hard circles, triangles and grids.

Then the pedigree.

In 1945, months after Kandinsky died, Rebay hung it in his memorial show in New York. The art historian Brenda Richardson credits that show with helping Barnett Newman find his direction.

Last year it was a highlight of a Kandinsky show at Museum Barberini in Germany. This year it hung in the Calder exhibition at Fondation Louis Vuitton in Paris.

The TLDR:

*The record was $44.8 million, and bidding started above it

*It was the first Kandinsky owned by the woman who built the Guggenheim's collection

*The museum sold it for £22,000, saying it had no room to hang it

*It comes from his first months at the Bauhaus, the start of his most famous style

Later in the night, Klimt's lake painting, with the same $60-80 million estimate, made $82.3 million. The Kandinsky still finished on top.

The Guggenheim had 170 Kandinskys and sold 50 to free up space.

If you held 170 works by one artist, how many would you sell?

~CdM

candidates.text:
My colleague Tyler Horner has been digging into our CTV incrementality tests and put numbers behind why you should look at marginal efficiency over average efficiency.

Here’s the comparison most teams make:
-> CTV’s efficiency vs. the brand’s average dollar in its other channels: 0.56x
-> Easy conclusion: “CTV is half as efficient. Not worth it.”

Now the comparison that matches the decision you’re actually making. For brands that tested CTV and also ran a spend test in another channel:
-> The next dollar in that core channel: 0.50x of its average
-> CTV: 0.49x of that same average
-> CTV vs. your next dollar: 0.98x

In this reframe CTV shifts from being about half as efficient to roughly even.

Important to also consider the upside with more effort. 

On Meta and Google, teams test thousands of creatives per month, try new bidding strategies and audiences, and make weekly adjustments. 

CTV often gets one spot that runs for months with very little in-flight optimization. We’re grading a channel we barely optimize against channels we optimize constantly, then blaming the channel for the gap in efficiency.

If CTV already comes out roughly even with your next Meta dollar while getting a fraction of the attention, then how well could it work after a roadmap of optimizations and retests?
